title: Listening practice: A conversation, a science talk and a presentation
description: Three recordings: two students talk about a late morning, a teacher explains a process in science, and a student presents on a trade network.

stimuli.title: Listen: Two students talk before class

turns.speaker: Diego
turns.text: Mei, you missed the first ten minutes of math. What happened?

turns.speaker: Mei
turns.text: You won't believe it. First, my alarm didn't go off because the power went out during the night, so I woke up late. Then I rushed out of the house, but when I got to the stop, the bus had already left. So I waited for the next one, but it never came. Finally, my neighbor, Mr. Okafor, saw me standing there and gave me a ride. He dropped me at the front door, and I ran straight to the office to get a late pass.

turns.speaker: Diego
turns.text: Wow. Do you want to copy my notes?

stimuli.script: Diego: Mei, you missed the first ten minutes of math. What happened? Mei: You won't believe it. First, my alarm didn't go off because the power went out during the night, so I woke up late. Then I rushed out of the house, but when I got to the stop, the bus had already left. So I waited for the next one, but it never came. Finally, my neighbor, Mr. Okafor, saw me standing there and gave me a ride. He dropped me at the front door, and I ran straight to the office to get a late pass. Diego: Wow. Do you want to copy my notes? Mei: Yes, please. Thanks, Diego!

stimuli.title: Listen: A science talk

turns.speaker: Teacher
turns.text: Have you ever noticed that on a sunny afternoon at the beach, the wind usually blows from the water toward the land? Here's why. During the day, the sun warms both the sand and the ocean, but the land heats up much faster than the water does. As a result, the air above the land becomes warmer than the air above the sea. Warm air is less dense than cool air, so it rises. When the warm air rises, it leaves an area of lower pressure near the ground. The cooler air over the water is denser, so it moves in to fill that space. We feel that moving air as a sea breeze. After sunset, the process reverses, because the land cools faster than the water does, and then the breeze blows from the land toward the sea.

stimuli.title: Listen: A student presentation

turns.speaker: Student
turns.text: Today I'll explain why the Silk Road mattered. First of all, the Silk Road wasn't one road. It was a network of trade routes that connected China with lands around the Mediterranean Sea, and people used it for more than a thousand years. It got its name from silk, which many places valued highly, but merchants also traded spices and glass. Here's something surprising: most merchants never traveled the whole way. Instead, goods passed through many hands, from one trader to the next. As a result, cities along the route, such as Samarkand, grew wealthy because they were good places to rest, trade, and exchange news. Finally, ideas moved along with goods. For example, the knowledge of how to make paper traveled west from China. So the Silk Road didn't only move products; it also connected people and spread knowledge.

items.stem: Why did Mei miss her first bus?

options.text: Her alarm did not go off.
The next bus never came to her stop.
She stopped at the office first.
Her neighbor drove past the stop.

distractors.b: That happened later. She waited for the next bus only after she had already missed the first one.
distractors.c: The office came at the end, after she finally reached school.
distractors.d: Her neighbor helped her after she had missed the bus, not before.

items.explanation: Mei says her alarm didn't go off because the power went out, so she woke up late and the bus had already left when she reached the stop.

support.clue: Listen to Mei's first sentence after the word First. It tells what started the problem.
support.model: Mentor example. "Jin was late to the picnic because his train was delayed by a storm." A reason follows the word because. Listen for Mei's first reason.

misconceptions.d: mixes up the problem with the rescue

items.stem: Match each part of Mei's morning to what happened.
items.explanation: Mei says the first bus had already left when she reached the stop, the second bus never came, and her neighbor Mr. Okafor gave her a ride.

support.clue: Listen for the words First, Then, So, and Finally. Match each bus or person with the words next to it.
support.frame: The first bus ______. The second bus ______. Mr. Okafor ______.
support.model: Mentor example. A student says: "The printer ran out of ink, the stapler jammed, and the teacher lent us a new one." You can match each object or person with what happened. Do the same for the two buses and Mr. Okafor.

items.stem: Put the steps of a sea breeze in order.

items.text: Cooler air from the sea moves in
The land heats up faster than the water
A low-pressure area forms near the ground
The air above the land becomes warmer

items.explanation: The land heats faster, so the air above it warms, the warm air rises, a low-pressure area forms near the ground, and cooler air from the sea moves in to fill the space.

support.clue: Listen for the linking phrases As a result, so, and When. Each one connects one step to the next.
support.model: Mentor example. "The pot heats the soup, so bubbles form. When bubbles rise, steam leaves the pot. As a result, the lid rattles." Each step causes the next step. Put the steps in the talk in order the same way.

facts: During the day land heats up faster than water.
Warm air is less dense than cool air and rises.
Cooler, denser air from over the sea moves in to replace the rising air, which is felt as a sea breeze.

items.stem: According to the teacher, why does warm air rise?

options.text: It is heavier than cool air.
The ocean pushes it upward.
The sun pulls it toward the sky.
It is less dense than cool air.

distractors.a: The teacher says warm air is less dense, not heavier.
distractors.b: The teacher says warm air rises because it is less dense. She does not say the ocean pushes it.
distractors.c: The sun heats the land; the teacher never says it pulls air.

items.explanation: The teacher says warm air is less dense than cool air, so it rises.

support.clue: Listen right after the teacher says the air above the land becomes warmer. Notice the word so.
support.frame: Warm air rises because it is ______ than cool air.
support.model: Mentor example. "A balloon filled with helium floats up because helium is lighter than the air around it." The reason compares two things. Find how the teacher compares warm air and cool air.

facts: Warm air is less dense than cool air, so it rises.

misconceptions.b: misreads the role of the sea

items.stem: What happens to the breeze after sunset, and why?

options.text: It stops because the sea gets warmer.
It reverses because the land cools faster than the water.
It reverses because the water cools faster than the land.
It gets stronger because the land stays warm.

distractors.a: The breeze does not stop; the teacher says the process reverses.
distractors.c: The teacher says the land cools faster, not the water.
distractors.d: After sunset the land cools faster, so it does not stay warm.

items.explanation: The teacher says that after sunset the process reverses because the land cools faster than the water, so the breeze blows from land to sea.

support.clue: Listen to the last sentence of the talk. Notice the words reverses and because.
support.frame: After sunset, the breeze ______ because one surface ______ faster than the other.
support.model: Mentor example. "In winter the lake freezes at the edges first, because shallow water cools faster than deep water, so skaters stay near the shore." The speaker explains a change by comparing two things. Explain the change in the breeze the same way.

facts: After sunset land cools faster than water, so the breeze reverses and blows from land toward the sea (a land breeze).

misconceptions.d: thinks the land keeps its heat

items.stem: How does the presenter correct a common idea about the Silk Road?

options.text: It was many routes, not one road.
It was one short road, not a long route.
It carried only silk, never other goods.
It lasted for one hundred years only.

distractors.b: The presenter says it connected China with lands around the Mediterranean Sea, so it was not one short road.
distractors.c: The presenter says merchants also traded spices and glass.
distractors.d: The presenter says people used it for more than a thousand years.

items.explanation: The presenter says the Silk Road was not one road but a network of trade routes connecting China with lands around the Mediterranean Sea.

support.clue: Listen to the second sentence of the talk. The speaker begins with the words "First of all."
support.model: Mentor example. "The Internet is not one computer; it is many computers linked together." A speaker can correct a common idea and then give the real description. Listen for how the presenter describes the Silk Road.

facts: The Silk Road was a network of trade routes connecting China with lands around the Mediterranean Sea.
It was used for over a thousand years.

items.stem: According to the presenter, why did cities like Samarkand grow wealthy?

options.text: They made most of the world's silk.
Every merchant who traveled the whole route stopped there.
They were good places to rest, trade, and share news.
They were the place where paper was invented.

distractors.a: The speaker says silk was valued but never says these cities made it.
distractors.b: The speaker says most merchants never traveled the whole way.
distractors.d: The speaker says paper-making knowledge came from China and does not link it to Samarkand.

items.explanation: The presenter says cities such as Samarkand grew wealthy because they were good places to rest, trade, and exchange news.

support.clue: Listen to the sentence that begins As a result. Notice the word because.
support.frame: Cities like Samarkand grew wealthy because they were ______ for ______.
support.model: Mentor example. "The mountain village became famous because climbers needed a place to prepare for the hike." A place becomes important because of what people do there. Explain why Samarkand grew in the same way.

facts: Samarkand was a major trading city on the Silk Road.
The knowledge of how to make paper traveled west from China along trade routes.

misconceptions.a: assumes the cities produced the silk

items.stem: What does the presenter mean by "goods passed through many hands"?

options.text: Merchants carried every item the whole way.
Many traders bought and resold goods along the route.
Goods were carried only by hand, never by animals.
Only a few trusted traders could sell silk.

distractors.a: The presenter says most merchants never traveled the whole way.
distractors.c: The phrase describes trading from one person to the next, not how goods were carried.
distractors.d: The presenter describes many traders, not a few.

items.explanation: The presenter explains that goods passed from one trader to the next, so many traders handled the goods along the route.

support.clue: Listen to the sentence that begins Instead. It explains the phrase.
support.frame: "Goods passed through many hands" means that ______ ______ ______.
support.model: Mentor example. "The message passed from student to student down the row" means each person told the next person. Explain a phrase by saying what really happens. Explain the presenter's phrase the same way.

facts: Along the Silk Road most merchants did not travel the whole route; goods were traded from one trader to the next.
